title: How to Practice Radical Acceptance
subtitle: It's a practice that takes practice.
body_html:
When I first heard about radical acceptance, it seemed like total BS. You want me to accept what I cannot change? No, thank you. I'm gonna fight as hard as I can. I'm a fighter, I would scream silently inside my own defiant mind.

Start with a simple definition. Acceptance… has definitions myriad, many of which are lacking.

Leaving aside the fact that the example sentences are comical in their ability to induce existential angst in me, personally, the “willingness to tolerate a difficult or unpleasant situation” is probably the closest to what we're talking about with radical acceptance, but so very not quite.

Radical acceptance, borrowed from Buddhism, was unfortunately pigeonholed as part of therapy and has been limited to those unpleasant situations conceptually.

a conscious effort to acknowledge and honor difficult situations and emotions. Fully accepting things as they are, instead of ignoring, avoiding, or wishing the situation were different, can be a critical step in moving through a difficult experience to experiencing more meaning.

And that's not sufficient.

Radical acceptance is the practice of accepting what is. What's happening now is what's happening now.

Now, or “the moment,” can be sliced infinitely thin. We can all understand that in a nanosecond, there's not much we can do. It's below the scale at which we have the ability to exercise volitional control. Longer moments give us the idea that we can do something about them. One second, one minute, one hour, one day, I'll offer the tantalizing promise that we can exercise our control over them. We can bend those moments to our will. This, unfortunately, is also kind of a con job, because most of the most important things in life we actually don't have any ability to control the course of. Who you meet, who you fall in love with, who lives, who dies, which earthquake up ends everything, which tsunami wipes everything that mattered to hundreds of thousands of people off the face of the earth in moments, none of those things are under our personal control.

The idea of radical acceptance is most useful in reminding us that the only thing we're able to control totally is our ability to accept that what is happening now is happening now.

The thing the therapeutic approaches leave out is how important it is to recognize that what's happening now might be great, it might be the best day of your life, it might be the single most important moment you've ever encountered. This, too, shall pass. When you focus on radically accepting only bad things, you don't get enough practice radically accepting everything.

When you focus only on radically accepting important things, you don't get enough practice doing it. Radical acceptance is hard. It's the only truly potent ability we have, as individuals, the ability to accept reality. Accepting reality or not accepting reality is completely within our power. Changing it, that's a different matter.

So my proposition, to us all, is that in encountering reality, on a routine basis, we should practice accepting it. We should set up an entire obstacle course throughout the day with the things we're gonna need to accept, ideally, in small bites. Getting lots of practice accepting reality prepares us to accept reality when it's really good or really bad.

When we have practice accepting what is, we can do it; when we do not, it causes us endless suffering.

Manifesto aside, now comes practical advice.

How do you get practice accepting? Well, here's what I've done.

In the morning, you know that phone that you carry around all the time? Which you bring to the bathroom with you? You're going to use it, but this time for good.

You're gonna set, randomly, throughout your day, three alarms.

10:50 AM. 1:36 PM. 6:19 PM.

I just made those numbers up. The phone alarm is gonna go off. And like a dialectical Pomodoro, at that moment, whatever you were doing will end. It doesn't matter for how long. You're gonna accept that it's over. Whatever you were doing, it's done.

Now, the length of the time that it's over doesn't really matter. You just have to accept that whatever you're working on has reached its conclusion. Maybe you were cleaning up the kitchen. Perhaps you were in the middle of a Zoom call. Maybe you were trying to finish a budget. Maybe you were making love to the most important lover you've ever met.

All of it, put it down. For one moment, for a fraction of a second, for an hour, but when the alarm goes off, you're accepting that it's over.

Maybe you were angry? You get to drop that. Perhaps you were happy, but that too falls away like sand.

You do this every day. Every day, you have a number of moments throughout the day where, to the degree of practicality, you radically accept that whatever was happening has reached its natural conclusion. Or, it's unnatural conclusion. And you walk away. Maybe you can't walk away from a business meeting, but you can walk away from how you felt about it in that moment. You can close your eyes, for just a moment, and accept that whatever you felt as melted, and you returned to that next moment, New.

That's it, that's the whole practice. You do it every day of your entire life, and that way, when something jumps out from behind a boulder, or lightning strikes from above, and you have to accept something truly challenging, your practice, your honed, you're ready. You're ready to accept that you met the love of your life. You're ready to accept that you lost a job. You're ready to accept a devastating loss of someone close to you. You're ready to accept the world isn't as you'd like it to be.

You don't get practice accepting if you don't do some accepting — radically accept the moment as it is, as many times as you can. It's not just about good things, it's not just about big things, and you're gonna have a hard time doing it for big bad things if you've never practiced it before. Think of it like a piano player, a virtuoso, slowing down the movement of their hands, so they can get that Rachmaninov passage just right, or the sniper at the range, for their job in the military, slowing down the motion of reloading the chamber so that they can get their aim just right.

We do these things as high-level professionals because we want to be good at them. When the time comes, we want to be able to deliver. Jazz musicians run boring scales all day, nice and slow, so that they can improvise beautifully at whatever tempo.

Slow down your acceptance, repeat your acceptance, except, and then accept again, when you find yourself letting it slip, and turning back to the feelings of anger, pleasure, rage, or whatever it was. Accept even your lack of acceptance.

But do it, on repeat, so that when it matters, you’ll be really good at it.
